title: Exchange accounts in an inheritance: what to do first, avoiding recovery scams, and why the seed phrase doesn't apply
plain:
Finding emails from an exchange like Coinbase means you've found a real asset to track — but do not try to reset passwords yet. You are not the account owner in the eyes of the exchange, and resets at this stage can trigger locks that slow everything down. Account recovery is a legal and identity process — do it deliberately with documents in hand. Today, just note that the account exists and keep the statements: save the emails, screenshots of balances, and any monthly statements so you can show what was there.

Be very careful with anyone who contacts you first. If a support chat offers to recover the account if you 'verify a code' they text you, that is a classic scam pattern — no legitimate exchange asks you to read back codes from an inbound contact. Contact the exchange only through its official website yourself — never through a link or chat that contacted you. Type the web address yourself or use a bookmark you made from a trusted source, and share no codes with anyone.

When you are ready to pursue the account, bring death certificate and estate documents through the official process — exchanges have a dedicated route for deceased account holders. Do not pose as the account owner; the official process is how the exchange legally confirms who may act for the estate.

Is the bitcoin in his Coinbase account backed up by the seed phrase you found? No — exchange accounts are custodial: the company holds the keys, not a seed phrase of yours. The account is accessed with login and identity documents, not seed words. That seed phrase matters only for any separate self-custody wallets you find, and it should never be typed into any exchange site.

Keep the two tracks separate in your inventory: one entry for the custodial exchange account, which is recovered through the legal process, and one for self-custody wallets, which are recovered through the backups and devices. Mixing them up is what leads people to try seed phrases on exchange logins — which never works and puts the backup at risk.
technical:
Exchange-held balances are custodial: the exchange controls the keys and its internal ledger, and the account balance is an obligation owed to the account holder (now the estate). Access runs through authentication plus identity and estate verification — a death certificate and documents establishing legal authority — via the exchange's official deceased-account process. Do not initiate password resets before this paperwork is ready; premature reset attempts can trip anti-fraud locks and complicate verification. All contact must be self-initiated at the exchange's officially published domain; inbound chats, links, emails, or calls offering 'recovery' are phishing vectors, and no legitimate exchange requests read-back of SMS or one-time codes.

Seed phrases (BIP-39 backups) restore only self-custody wallets; they have no relationship to custodial account balances and must never be entered or dictated into any website, chat, or verification flow. Maintain two distinct inventory tracks — custodial accounts (legal/identity recovery) and self-custody holdings (backup/device recovery) — since the recovery paths, timelines, and risks differ.
